name: Trauma, Burns & Surgery
sub: ATLS, damage control, burns, spine, pelvic, perioperative

cards.q: What is the primary survey sequence in ATLS 11?
cards.a: xABCDE: x control of exsanguinating external haemorrhage first (tourniquet, wound packing, pelvic binder), then A airway with cervical spine protection, B breathing and ventilation, C circulation with haemorrhage control, D disability (GCS, pupils), E exposure and environmental control.

cards.q: What are the haemorrhage classes in ATLS?
cards.a: Class I <15% (<750 mL), II 15–30%, III 30–40% (hypotension, tachycardia >120), IV >40% (critical). Young patients may compensate until class III.
cards.src: ATLS 10th ed. (ATLS 11, 2025, revises content; reviewer to confirm)

cards.q: What is permissive hypotension in trauma?
cards.a: Target SBP about 80–90 mmHg (MAP 50–60) until haemorrhage control in penetrating torso trauma; avoid in traumatic brain injury (maintain SBP ≥110). ATLS 11 pairs it with early blood products (balanced 1:1:1 or low-titre whole blood where available) and minimal crystalloid as a bridge.

cards.q: What are the signs of tension pneumothorax and the treatment?
cards.a: Respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation (late), absent breath sounds, distended neck veins. Needle decompression (5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line) then chest drain.
cards.src: ATLS 10th ed. (ATLS 11, 2025, available; reviewer to confirm site)

cards.q: List life-threatening thoracic injuries to identify in the primary survey.
cards.a: Airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with pulmonary contusion, and cardiac tamponade.

cards.q: What is the Beck's triad and how is tamponade managed?
cards.a: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins. Treat with resuscitative thoracotomy or pericardiocentesis/pericardial window.

cards.q: What are the indications for emergency thoracotomy?
cards.a: Penetrating thoracic trauma with loss of signs of life in the field or ED; blunt trauma with witnessed arrest has poor outcomes.

cards.q: What is the Parkland formula for burn resuscitation?
cards.a: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA of Ringer's lactate over 24 hours; half in the first 8 hours (from the time of burn) and half over the following 16 hours; titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h.

cards.q: Describe the rule of nines in adults.
cards.a: Head 9%, each arm 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%.

cards.q: What are the signs of inhalation injury?
cards.a: Facial burns, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor. Intubate early when airway oedema is anticipated and give 100% oxygen for carbon monoxide.

cards.q: When is escharotomy needed?
cards.a: Circumferential full-thickness limb or chest burns with compartment syndrome (loss of pulses, impaired ventilation).

cards.q: What are the Nexus low-risk criteria for cervical spine imaging?
cards.a: No midline tenderness, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and no painful distracting injury.

cards.q: What is neurogenic shock?
cards.a: Hypotension with bradycardia from cervical or high thoracic cord injury due to loss of sympathetic tone. Treat with fluids and vasopressors; target MAP 85–90 mmHg for 5–7 days in acute SCI.

cards.q: How do you manage unstable pelvic fractures with haemorrhage?
cards.a: Pelvic binder at the greater trochanters, massive transfusion, preperitoneal packing or angioembolisation, and external fixation.

cards.q: What are the 6 Ps of compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Pain (out of proportion), pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, pulselessness (late), and poikilothermia; confirm with compartment pressures (>30 mmHg or ΔP <30) and perform fasciotomy.

cards.q: What is the FAST examination?
cards.a: Focused ultrasound of the pericardium, Morison's pouch, splenorenal space and pelvis (plus bilateral chest views in eFAST) to detect free fluid or pneumothorax.

cards.q: How is fat embolism syndrome recognised?
cards.a: Hypoxia, neurological changes and petechial rash 24–72 hours after long-bone fracture; supportive care with early fixation.

cards.q: What is the management for postoperative ileus versus obstruction?
cards.a: Ileus: correct electrolytes, minimise opioids, nasogastric decompression if vomiting. Obstruction: CT imaging, surgical review and resuscitation.

cards.q: Which anaesthetic or surgical problems commonly cause postoperative ICU admission?
cards.a: Haemorrhage, sepsis, cardiac complications, respiratory failure and prolonged ventilation; identify risk early using tools such as ARISCAT and RCRI.

cards.q: A trauma patient has SBP 70 mmHg, a distended abdomen and positive FAST. What is the best next step?
o: Activate massive transfusion and proceed to laparotomy
cards.e: A haemodynamically unstable patient with positive FAST requires haemorrhage control; avoid delays for CT and large crystalloid volumes.

cards.q: A 70-kg patient has 40% TBSA burns. What fluid volume does Parkland calculate for the first 8 hours?
cards.e: 4 × 70 × 40 = 11,200 mL in 24 hours; half (5,600 mL) in the first 8 hours.

cards.q: What else changed in ATLS 11?
cards.a: Damage-control resuscitation is emphasised (balanced 1:1:1 or low-titre group O whole blood, crystalloid kept to a minimum as a bridge, tranexamic acid within 3 hours as 1 g plus 1 g infusion); spine motion restriction is selective and criteria-based with less reliance on rigid collars; stronger focus on team communication and leadership.
